placement.position_note: Interpretive placement on a GENERATED lot, not a recovered parcel. The lot geometry is the K7 plat module's — this project has never read Thompson's numbering off a sheet, and the side lot lines and the alley are conjectural even where the block face is not. The building stands 5.0 m back from its alley edge, which is a typology for the period and not a measurement of this lot. The whole footprint — not its centre — is tested against the platted street corridors, against its own lot lines and against every other footprint in the dataset, so no invented building of this parcel stands in the roadway; clearing the roadway is not the same as standing on a recovered lot.

occupants.value: The Sabine household — a documented forwarding and commission, unplaced in the town
occupants.note: SEATED BY THE PLACEMENT POLICY'S PLATTED DEAL (data/reconstruction/1835_platted_seats.json, dealt by T-1613 and carried onto this roof by T-1685; liberties L270 and L276). NO SOURCE PLACES THIS HOUSEHOLD HERE, OR ANYWHERE. Its own record gives a name and no address — no street, no lot and not even a division — so both halves of its band were dealt rather than read, and the lot under this roof is the policy's labourer_dwellings clause answered on the committed plat: blk_randolph_market#00, fronting randolph, a standing roof of family D2 the clause admits. THE SOURCES BELOW CARRY THE NAME AND NOTHING ELSE. The roof's own existence, position and footprint remain conjectural and are unchanged by the seating — it is still a count-unit of the 665-roof programme, adopted rather than raised, so nothing was drawn off the reconstruction order book. The household's id is carried in resident_assignment rather than in this prose, because tools/generate_dooryard_pickets.py admits a lot for a garden on an id appearing HERE and a keeper a policy deal seats is not a measurement of anybody's garden.

residents.why: the roof T-1613 dealt this household, joined here and not re-argued
residents.basis: HOUSED HERE BY THE DEAL, NOT RECORDED HERE (L354). The sources stop short of 1 July 1835 for this household and nothing puts it anywhere else; the town's rule (T-1386) counts it present, and no source says where it slept. The roof is the invention and the people are not.

persons.name: Wm. Sabine
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'WM. SABINE' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the American of 13 June 1835, column 5. The corpus associates the name with North Water Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `forwarding_and_commission` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “W. Sabine” (f1839_v0633, printed page 45, ward 6, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Sabine' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins W. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name Wm. Sabine as a forwarding and commission at Chicago 1 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

citations.citation: Robert Fergus, Fergus' Directory of the City of Chicago, 1839 (Chicago: Fergus Printing Company, 1876) — Fergus' Historical Series No. 2; read from the Allen County Public Library Genealogy Center scan on the Internet Archive
what_it_supplies: A name, a trade and a street for 1,655 entries in the city of 1839 — the closest address list to 1835 this project can reach.
A trade for 976 of them at a stated street, which compiles into 102 street faces (Lake 199, Clark 94, North Water 83, South Water 72).

On printed page 37: six churches with their ministers, fifteen hotels, the public offices around the Public Square, the land office, the lighthouse, the theatre, two named building rows, the Dutch Settlement, and the fire that took the Tremont House on 27 October 1839.
what_it_does_not_supply: An 1835 residency. Four years late, and the ratified ladder never makes a resident from a later listing alone.

An address number that means anything, off Lake street. Fergus writes on printed page 3 that no street but Lake was numbered in 1839 and that 'the numbers now given are those of the present day' — 1876's. Only the street name crosses.
A count of its own entries. The volume states no number of names anywhere, so a reading of it cannot be closed against the book the way a census sheet closes against its printed totals.
